characters.description: A hobbit of the Shire, Bilbo's younger cousin and heir, who inherits Bag End and Bilbo's old ring when the old hobbit departs. Thoughtful and decent, he loves the Shire's quiet life but comes to shoulder a burden that will carry him far from home.
characters.name: Frodo Baggins

characters.description: Frodo's gardener and steadfast friend, a plain, loyal hobbit with a love of old tales and elves. Caught listening at the window while Gandalf reveals the ring's danger, he is enlisted as Frodo's companion and simply refuses to be parted from his master.
characters.name: Samwise Gamgee

characters.description: The wandering wizard, an old friend of Bilbo's, whose fireworks delight the Shire. Long uneasy about Bilbo's ring, he investigates its history and returns with grim news, setting Frodo on the road and guiding the growing effort against the rising Enemy.
characters.name: Gandalf

characters.description: Now very old but strangely unwearied, the hero of an earlier adventure. At his birthday party he vanishes using his ring and leaves the Shire for good, passing Bag End and - reluctantly, at Gandalf's urging - the ring itself on to Frodo.
characters.name: Bilbo Baggins

characters.description: A weather-worn Ranger first met at the inn in Bree, where he goes by Strider. Grim and watchful, he proves a friend and guides the hobbits toward Rivendell; he is far more than the rough wanderer he seems, being the long-hidden heir of ancient kings.
characters.name: Aragorn

characters.description: A capable, practical young hobbit and Frodo's cousin, one of the friends who has quietly guessed Frodo's secret and insists on sharing the journey rather than being left safely behind.
characters.name: Meriadoc Brandybuck

characters.description: Frodo's young, cheerful cousin, quick of tongue and eager for the road, who sets out with Frodo and Sam when they leave the Shire and becomes one of the company of travellers.
characters.name: Peregrin Took

characters.description: A proud, valiant warrior from the southern land of Gondor who comes to the Council of Elrond seeking help against the Enemy. Brave and well-meaning, he joins the company but is increasingly troubled by the thought of using the ring's power to defend his people.
characters.name: Boromir

characters.description: The ancient, wise, and beautiful elven Lady who rules the golden wood of Lothlórien and shelters the weary company. She tests each of them, gives them gifts for the road, and shows Frodo a glimpse of things that may come to pass in her mirror.
characters.name: Galadriel

characters.description: The unseen Dark Lord who forged the One Ring long ago to master all the others, and who now bends his will to recovering it. Though he never appears in person, his shadow spreads out of the land of Mordor and his servants hunt the ring across the world.
characters.name: Sauron

recaps.ending: Fellowship ends with the company broken at the falls of the great river Anduin. Boromir, overmastered by the ring's lure, tries to take it from Frodo; shaken, Frodo decides he must carry it to Mordor by himself rather than risk corrupting or endangering his friends. He slips away by boat, but Sam refuses to be left and forces his way aboard, so the two go east toward the Enemy's land together and alone. The rest of the Fellowship is left scattered and searching, unaware which way Frodo has gone. Gandalf is believed dead, lost in the deeps of Moria after his fall with the demon of fire. Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli remain on the western shore, while Boromir, Merry, and Pippin are elsewhere along the river, their fates unresolved as the book closes. The ring is still whole and still far from the fire; Sauron's power grows and his armies stir, but the Enemy does not yet know exactly where the ring is. The quest is now split into two strands, two hobbits creeping toward Mordor and the sundered remnant of the Fellowship left to face the coming war, both carried forward into the next book.
recaps.in_short: The hobbit Frodo Baggins inherits a magic ring from his cousin Bilbo, and the wizard Gandalf reveals it to be the One Ring of the Dark Lord Sauron, who is rising again and hunting for it. To keep it from the Enemy, Frodo leaves the Shire with his friends Sam, Merry, and Pippin, pursued by Sauron's Black Riders. After narrow escapes and a near-fatal wound at Weathertop, they reach Rivendell, where a council decides the ring must be destroyed in the fire of Mordor where it was made. Frodo volunteers, and a Fellowship of nine sets out to help him: Gandalf, the ranger Aragorn, Boromir of Gondor, the elf Legolas, the dwarf Gimli, and the four hobbits. Blocked by mountains, they pass through the mines of Moria, where Gandalf falls battling a demon of fire. Sheltered and counselled by the elf-lady Galadriel, they travel on by river. At the last, Boromir tries to seize the ring, and Frodo, fearing its power over his friends, resolves to go on alone; only Sam manages to follow him as the Fellowship breaks apart.

recaps.text: Years ago the hobbit Bilbo Baggins, on an adventure with dwarves and the wizard Gandalf, found a plain gold ring deep under the Misty Mountains and took it from the creature Gollum. It made its wearer invisible, and Bilbo kept it quietly for the rest of his long life, using it now and then and telling no one its worth. What neither he nor anyone in the Shire knew was that this was the One Ring, forged in secret ages past by the Dark Lord Sauron to control all the other Rings of Power and to dominate Middle-earth. The Ring was cut from Sauron's hand in an ancient war and lost for centuries, passing at last to Gollum and then, by chance, to Bilbo. Now, after long years of hiding and slow recovery, Sauron has taken shape again in the land of Mordor and is searching everywhere for his lost Ring, whose return would make him unstoppable. His hunt is beginning to reach toward the quiet corner of the world where the Ring has lain forgotten.

At his eleventy-first birthday party in the Shire, Bilbo Baggins slips the ring on before the astonished guests, vanishes, and leaves the district for good, bequeathing Bag End and the ring to his young cousin and heir, Frodo. The wizard Gandalf, uneasy about the ring, presses Bilbo to give it up before he goes, and Bilbo does so with difficulty. Years pass. Gandalf's growing fears drive him to research the ring's history, and he returns to warn Frodo of the truth: the plain little ring is the One Ring of the Dark Lord Sauron, who is rising again and searching for it. Gandalf tells how the creature Gollum, who once owned it, has been captured and questioned, and has spoken of the Shire and of the name Baggins, so the Enemy now knows where to look. The ring cannot stay in the Shire. Gandalf sets Frodo to leave secretly, making for the elf-haven of Rivendell, and Frodo prepares to slip away with his gardener Sam, who is caught eavesdropping and enlisted as a companion.

Frodo sells Bag End as a cover and sets out on foot with Sam and his cousin Pippin, aiming for Rivendell. Almost at once a black-cloaked rider sniffs after them along the road, one of the Enemy's servants. They dodge the pursuit with help from passing elves and from Farmer Maggot, and reach the edge of the Shire, where Frodo's friend Merry reveals that he and the others already know about the ring and mean to come too. To avoid the watched roads the hobbits cut through the Old Forest, where a malevolent old tree nearly swallows them until a strange, powerful being named Tom Bombadil rescues and shelters them. Leaving his house, they are trapped by a barrow-wight among the ancient grave-mounds; Bombadil frees them again, and from the barrow-hoard they take old daggers well suited to hobbit hands. Gandalf, meanwhile, has failed to meet them as promised, and the hobbits press on toward the village of Bree, uneasy and still hunted.

At the inn in Bree the hobbits use the name Underhill, but Frodo draws attention when he accidentally slips the ring on and vanishes before a crowd. A weathered Ranger called Strider warns them they are in danger and offers to guide them; a letter left by Gandalf confirms he can be trusted and reveals that Strider is really Aragorn. That night the Black Riders attack the hobbits' abandoned room, and the party flees Bree with Aragorn into the wild. At the hill of Weathertop the Riders assail them, and their leader stabs Frodo in the shoulder with a cursed blade before Aragorn drives them off with fire. Frodo sickens as a splinter works toward his heart. Aragorn hurries them onward, and near Rivendell they are met by an elf who sets Frodo on a swift horse. At the ford of the river the Riders close in, but a sudden flood, raised by the elves' power, sweeps them away as Frodo, barely conscious, is carried across to safety.

Frodo wakes in Rivendell, healed by Elrond of the wound that would have made him a wraith, and is joyfully reunited with Sam, his cousins, the aged Bilbo, and Gandalf, who explains that he was delayed by the treachery of a fellow wizard, Saruman. Elrond calls a great council, where the ring's long history is laid out and the danger of Sauron's return is weighed. Every alternative is rejected: the ring cannot be wielded for good without corrupting its bearer, cannot be hidden forever, and cannot be given to the sea or the elves. The only course is to unmake it in the fire where it was forged, deep in Sauron's own land of Mordor. Frodo, though it terrifies him, offers to carry the ring. A Fellowship of nine is chosen to go with him: Gandalf; Aragorn and Boromir, a lord of Gondor; the elf Legolas; the dwarf Gimli; and Frodo's three hobbit companions, Sam, Merry, and Pippin.

The Fellowship travels south in secret. Turned back by a savage snowstorm on the mountain pass of Caradhras, which some suspect is the work of an enemy, they take instead the long dark road beneath the mountains through the abandoned dwarf-realm of Moria. At its western gate a many-armed creature in a black pool nearly seizes Frodo before they get inside. Within the vast, silent halls they find the tomb of Balin and a record of how the dwarf-colony there was destroyed. Attacked by orcs and a cave-troll, they fight their way toward the eastern exit, but at the Bridge of Khazad-dum a Balrog, an ancient demon of fire and shadow, bars the way. Gandalf makes a stand on the narrow bridge and breaks it beneath the creature, but the Balrog's whip drags him down into the abyss as he falls, and he is lost. The grieving survivors escape into the daylight.

Leaderless and mourning Gandalf, the company comes to Lothlorien, a hidden elvish realm of great beauty and power ruled by the Lady Galadriel and Lord Celeborn. The elves shelter and heal them. Galadriel quietly tests the hearts of the Fellowship and, at their asking, shows Frodo and Sam visions in her mirror of things that were, are, and may yet come, including the Shire under threat. Frodo offers her the ring, but she refuses the temptation to take it and remains herself. Rested, the travellers are given boats, grey elvish cloaks that hide their wearers, waybread that sustains them on the road, and other parting gifts, among them a coil of rope for Sam and a phial holding a star's light for Frodo, to be a light in dark places. Gimli, at first wary of the elves, is won over and asks only for a strand of the Lady's hair. They set out down the great river Anduin, carried southward toward the borders of the enemy's country, the burden of the choice ahead growing heavier with every mile.

The Fellowship journeys down the Anduin, passing the towering carved kings that mark Gondor's ancient border, and lands to decide their course: onward to the fire of Mordor, or aside to the defence of Gondor's city, Minas Tirith. Boromir, who has come to believe the ring should be used as a weapon to save his people, follows Frodo apart and tries first to persuade and then to seize it. Frightened at how the ring can twist even a brave and honorable man, Frodo puts it on to escape him and resolves to go on to Mordor alone, rather than lead his friends to ruin or let the ring corrupt them. He means to slip away by boat unseen, but Sam guesses his plan, wades after him, and refuses to be left behind. The two cross the river together and set off eastward alone, while the rest of the company, searching for Frodo, is scattered, and the book ends with the Fellowship broken.

characters.description: A boy taken into a research compound in the far north after the solar flares and the disease that followed. He was born Stephen and renamed Thomas by the people who took him; he is one of a small number of children the illness cannot infect, which is the only reason he is alive and locked up. Curious, argumentative and desperately lonely, he spends his first years in a single room with a caretaker, a window, and lessons he is not permitted to question.
characters.name: Thomas

characters.description: The staff member assigned to Thomas when he first arrives: the man who brings his meals, runs his lessons and administers his tests, and who declines to answer anything that actually matters.
characters.name: Randall

characters.description: A girl of Thomas's age held elsewhere in the same compound, born Deedee and renamed by the organization that took her. She reaches Thomas first as a voice inside his own head, the two of them being the subjects of an implant that lets them speak mind to mind, and for years she is the only friend he has. She is quicker than Thomas to accept the rules of the place and better than he is at working out what the adults want to hear.
characters.name: Teresa

characters.description: A senior official in the organization running the compound, composed and unfailingly reasonable, who speaks to the children as though they were colleagues rather than subjects. She regards the program as justified by the cure it is chasing and says so without apology.
characters.name: Ava Paige

characters.description: One of the immune children in the compound, and one of the first Thomas meets once he is allowed contact with the rest of the group. Even-tempered and easy to like, he holds the others together where louder boys divide them.
characters.name: Newt

characters.description: An immune boy in the same group, blunt, physically confident and openly contemptuous of the tests the children are put through. He treats defiance as a sport, which makes him popular with the others and a standing problem for the staff.
characters.name: Minho

characters.description: The chancellor of the organization during Thomas's childhood, and the man whose authority sets the pace and the limits of the program.
characters.name: Kevin Anderson

characters.description: One of the older boys among the immune subjects, serious and self-contained, who takes responsibility for the younger ones without being asked to. The staff notice that about him too.
characters.name: Alby

characters.description: A boy in Thomas's group, wary and quick to take offense, who never quite trusts Thomas or the access to the adults that Thomas is given.
characters.name: Gally

characters.description: A much younger boy living inside the compound, talkative and starved of company, who attaches himself to Thomas. He is far too young for what the older children are being prepared for, and Thomas treats keeping him out of it as a personal obligation.
characters.name: Chuck

characters.description: A boy from the second group of subjects the organization runs in parallel, and that group's equivalent of Thomas, carrying the same implant.
characters.name: Aris

characters.description: A girl from the second group, paired with Aris in the way Thomas is paired with Teresa.
characters.name: Rachel

characters.description: A girl in the second group of subjects, kept apart from the boys for most of Thomas's childhood. She was born Elizabeth and is Newt's younger sister; the organization separated the two of them, renamed her, and did not intend either of them to find out.
characters.name: Sonya

characters.description: One of the leaders among the girls in the second group, level-headed and used to speaking for the others.
characters.name: Harriet

recaps.ending: The maze is complete and running, and the organization decides that its two implanted subjects are the last variables it needs. Thomas and Teresa agree to be inserted. Before the memory procedure they settle on a plan: once inside, with everything taken from them, they will work to break the maze rather than solve it, and leave themselves whatever cues they can manage. That agreement is where their friendship ends rather than where it holds. Teresa maintains that everything WICKED has done is justified by the cure at the end of it, Thomas no longer believes that, and neither talks the other around. Their friends have already gone in ahead of them, sent up one at a time with Thomas and Teresa in the room while it was done, including Newt, whom Thomas knows is not immune and is being used as a control, and Chuck, whom Thomas failed to keep off the list. Thomas is wiped and sent up in the Box next to last, arriving in a Glade full of boys he helped put there, none of whom will remember him. Teresa follows the day after, and the program stops sending anyone. The final pages hand straight off to the opening of The Maze Runner, with the reader now knowing who designed the Maze and who chose the people inside it.
recaps.in_short: A prequel covering Thomas's childhood inside WICKED. Taken as a small boy after the flares and the Flare virus destroyed the world he was born into, and renamed from Stephen because he is immune, he grows up in a locked room in a compound in the far north with only a caretaker for company, and later a girl's voice in his head: Teresa, wired to him by an implant. Let out among the other immune children, he grows up with Newt, Minho, Alby and Gally while the adults test and operate on them, and eventually learns what it is all for. An enormous maze is being built to put immune minds under sustained pressure so their brain patterns can be recorded. Thomas and Teresa are brought in to help design and run it, which costs them the trust of everyone they grew up with. The trials begin, and Thomas watches his friends have their memories stripped and be sent into the Glade, Newt among them despite not being immune, and Chuck despite being a child. Finally Thomas and Teresa go in themselves, planning to sabotage the maze from inside, and the memory wipe closes the book where The Maze Runner opens.

recaps.text: The Fever Code is a prequel, published after the original trilogy and set in the years immediately before The Maze Runner. It assumes the reader already knows the shape of that series: solar flares wrecked the planet, an engineered virus called the Flare followed and destroys the mind of anyone it infects, and an organization known as WICKED responded by collecting children who are immune to it and putting them through elaborate, deliberately cruel trials in the hope of mapping the brain patterns that resist the disease. Trilogy readers know that Thomas and Teresa arrived in the Glade with their memories stripped, that they had worked for WICKED beforehand, that they had a hand in designing the Maze, and that this is the thing the other Gladers found hardest to forgive. The earlier prequel, The Kill Order, showed how the virus came to be released and closed with an immune girl called Deedee being taken into the organization's care and renamed Teresa. This book fills the gap between the two. It covers Thomas's childhood inside WICKED from the day he is taken to the moment he goes up in the Box, and the answers it gives are to questions the trilogy left as gaps rather than as mysteries.

Thomas is taken from his mother in the aftermath of the flares. He is small enough that most of what he understands comes secondhand: the world burned, a disease followed, his mother has it and he does not. The people who take him give him a new name, having been born Stephen, and put him in a single room in a compound somewhere cold and remote. His entire contact with the world is a caretaker called Randall, who brings food, runs lessons, and refuses every question about why he is there or when he is leaving. Thomas is told, repeatedly and calmly, that he is important, that he is safe, and that whatever is being done to him is necessary. The chapters are dated, and the dates make it plain from the start that this will not be a short stay.

Years pass in the room. Thomas begins hearing a girl's voice inside his own head: Teresa, held elsewhere in the same building and carrying the same implant he does. The two of them talk constantly and privately and grow up as each other's only company. Thomas is eventually let out among the other immune children the organization has collected, including Newt and Minho, boys who have been in the compound as long as he has. The children are tested, measured and scanned, told they are the last hope of a species facing an incurable brain disease, and given no say in any part of it. They can tell the adults are building toward something specific, and nobody will tell them what it is.

Thomas settles into life among the other subjects and the group hardens into real friendships: Newt keeps the peace, Minho pushes against every rule, Alby takes charge of the younger ones. The testing escalates, and so does the surgery, with the children fitted with hardware in their brains that the staff describe as necessary instrumentation. They push back where they can, exploring parts of the compound they have not been shown and being punished when they are caught. Thomas begins to grasp the scale of the project: the organization is not treating the disease so much as trying to read the minds of the people it cannot touch, and that reading apparently requires its subjects to be kept under pressure.

The purpose becomes concrete. An enormous maze is under construction, and the children in the compound are the people who will be put inside it. Thomas and Teresa are singled out: because they already carry the implant, and because the adults judge them cooperative, they are given work alongside the researchers, with access to the plans, the site and the reasoning behind the design. The other children see exactly what that looks like from the outside. Newt learns that his younger sister has been in the compound the whole time, placed in a second group and given another name, and that nobody had any intention of telling him. Trust between Thomas and his friends starts to come apart, and Teresa's willingness to argue the organization's case does not help.

There are two programs running in parallel, a group of boys and a group of girls, each with its own maze and each with a pair of implanted subjects: Thomas and Teresa on one side, Aris and Rachel on the other. Thomas meets the girls' group, among them Harriet and Newt's sister, now called Sonya. He and Teresa spend years working on the maze itself, walking its corridors as they are built, helping shape the layout, and seeing the machines that will be turned loose inside it. Chuck, a small boy far too young for any of this, attaches himself to Thomas, and Thomas starts trying to keep his name off the lists. An attempt by the friends to get out of the compound fails, and the punishment for it is isolation.

Thomas spends a long stretch cut off from everyone and comes out of it changed, quieter and less willing to argue. The leadership presses on regardless: Chancellor Anderson and Ava Paige treat the trials as the only available route to a cure and the children's objections as something to be waited out. The maze is finished and stocked. Thomas is walked through how the insertions will work, one subject at a time with their memories removed and no explanation offered, and a supply lift bringing the next boy up at fixed intervals for as long as the trials run. He and Teresa are the two who will help operate it.

The trials begin. Alby goes in first, alone, with everything he knows taken from him. The rest follow at intervals, one at a time: Newt, Minho, Gally and the others Thomas grew up with. Thomas and Teresa are in the control rooms for all of it, watching friends be processed and sent up, and being seen doing it. Thomas learns something he keeps to himself, which is that Newt is not immune and is being sent into the maze anyway, as a control. Chuck's name comes up in spite of everything Thomas has done to keep it off the list, and Chuck goes in too, one of the last before the program's final pair.

With the maze running and only the last variables left to add, the organization tells Thomas and Teresa that they are going in themselves. They agree, and in the time they have left they make a plan: once inside, memories gone, they will work to break the maze rather than solve it, and leave themselves whatever prompts they can. The plan is the last thing they share. Teresa still holds that the trials are justified by the cure at the end of them, Thomas does not, and they part without settling it. Thomas is put through the memory procedure and sent up in the Box with nothing left but his name, into a Glade full of boys he helped put there and who remember none of it either. Teresa follows the day after, the last subject the program will ever send in. The book closes exactly where The Maze Runner opens.

characters.description: The physician of Fraser's Ridge, running a surgery out of a mountain cabin with home-made instruments, home-grown drugs and two centuries of knowledge she cannot explain to anyone. In her mid-fifties, practical and increasingly indispensable to the settlement, she is living toward a dated newspaper notice that says she and her husband will die in a fire on this land.
characters.name: Claire Fraser

characters.description: Laird of Fraser's Ridge, landlord to a scatter of Highland tenants and holder of a royal land grant that carries obligations to the Crown. He is a former Jacobite who has already fought one losing war for a king, he knows from his wife how this colony's quarrel with Britain ends, and he is trying to keep his people out of it for as long as he can.
characters.name: Jamie Fraser

characters.description: Claire and Jamie's daughter, an engineer by training stranded in a century with no engineering, raising a small son and steadily inventing what she can from memory. Tall, red-haired and blunt, she has chosen this life and this husband, and she carries a fear of the man who assaulted her that she has not put down.
characters.name: Brianna Fraser

characters.description: A twentieth-century historian and folk singer trying to make himself useful on an eighteenth-century mountain, where his scholarship is worth nothing and he cannot yet shoot, plough or fight. Married to Brianna and raising a child he has claimed without knowing whose he is, he is looking for a place of his own in his father-in-law's settlement.
characters.name: Roger MacKenzie

characters.description: Brianna's small son, a red-haired toddler, claimed and loved by Roger. Which of two men fathered him is a question nobody in the family can answer and nobody raises aloud.
characters.name: Jemmy

characters.description: Jamie's blind aunt, mistress of the rich River Run plantation, still managing the people around her by charm, money and information. She has arranged her own remarriage to suit herself and keeps her late husband's affairs, and their sources, firmly to herself.
characters.name: Jocasta Cameron

characters.description: The one-armed former prisoner who has become Jocasta Cameron's steward and is now to become her husband. Modest, kindly, and quietly overwhelmed by his change in fortune, he is loyal to Jamie above everyone.
characters.name: Duncan Innes

characters.description: Laoghaire's elder daughter, now Fergus's wife and a mother, settled near the Ridge. Sharp-tongued, hard-working and thoroughly acclimatised to frontier life, she has made her peace with Claire.
characters.name: Marsali Fraser

characters.description: Jamie's adopted son, a one-handed Frenchman raising a family on the edge of the settlement and making a living by his wits. Charming and adaptable, he chafes at how little the mountains reward charm.
characters.name: Fergus Fraser

characters.description: The small Scottish bondservant who came over with Brianna, now part of the Fraser household and devoted to her father, who is also on the Ridge. Nervous, dutiful and prone to fever, she has never entirely lived down the mistake she made about Roger.
characters.name: Lizzie Wemyss

characters.description: The royal governor of North Carolina, a capable administrator with a rebellion in his backcountry and a career to protect. He granted Jamie his land, commissioned him a colonel of militia, and expects the debt to be paid in men and obedience.
characters.name: William Tryon

characters.description: The Frasers' new housekeeper, a tiny, round, tireless woman who arrives with her husband and takes over the running of the house entirely. Endlessly talkative and formidably competent, she treats everyone on the Ridge as hers to feed and organise.
characters.name: Mrs. Bug

characters.description: The Irish pirate who robbed the Frasers on the river and assaulted Brianna, alive and at large in the colony. Charming in company and entirely indifferent to other people, he has money, a ship, and no reason to think anyone can touch him.
characters.name: Stephen Bonnet

characters.description: A young indentured hunter, barely into his teens, whom Claire first treated for a badly infected throat. Silent about his own history and an extraordinarily good shot, he is the sort of asset a mountain settlement badly needs, and he wants a place on the Ridge.
characters.name: Josiah Beardsley

characters.description: The woman of an isolated trading farm the militia calls at, heavily pregnant, evasive, and living in a house where something is badly wrong. What she has been doing there is discovered by Claire and Jamie rather than told.
characters.name: Fanny Beardsley

characters.description: Jamie's oldest English friend, a soldier turned Virginia planter, connected at court and a reliable correspondent about what London is thinking. His long-standing obligations to the Fraser family are known to Jamie and Claire and to almost nobody else.
characters.name: Lord John Grey

recaps.ending: After Alamance the family goes home to the Ridge, and Roger spends months relearning how to speak. His voice comes back as a ruined whisper, enough to preach and teach with but not to sing, and he builds a place for himself on the mountain out of what is left. He and Brianna decide to stay in the past rather than risk the stones. Jamie is bitten by a venomous snake and comes very near death; Claire keeps him alive through days of gangrene and fever. The last of the book turns on Jocasta Cameron's hidden Jacobite gold and on Stephen Bonnet, who is hunting it. The pursuit ends in a fight on the coast at Wylie's Landing, where Brianna shoots Bonnet in the head at close range; he falls into the water and no body is found. The question of Jemmy's father is left where it stands, and Roger has stopped needing an answer. Claire and Jamie return to Fraser's Ridge with the newspaper notice of their own deaths still years ahead of them and a war with Britain coming closer. The book closes with Jamie telling Claire that when the day comes that he must leave her, if his last words are not that he loves her, it will only be because he had no breath left to say them.
recaps.in_short: At a Highland gathering in North Carolina in 1770, Brianna and Roger are properly married, Jocasta Cameron is betrothed to Duncan Innes, and Governor Tryon commissions Jamie a colonel of militia and orders him to raise men against the Regulators, backcountry farmers in armed revolt. Jamie calls out his tenants under a burning cross in the old Highland fashion, and the militia marches twice, the first time ending without a battle and turning up the horrors of an isolated trading farm. The second march ends at Alamance in May 1771, where the Regulators are scattered and Roger, mistaken for one of them, is hanged; Jamie and Claire cut him down and Claire opens his throat to keep him alive. He survives without a voice. The rest of the book follows his slow recovery, the family's life on Fraser's Ridge, and a hunt for Stephen Bonnet, who is after Jocasta's hidden Jacobite gold. It ends with Brianna shooting Bonnet at Wylie's Landing and the family going home, with the fire that history promises them still in the future.

recaps.text: Previously, in the Outlander books: Claire Randall travelled from the twentieth century to 1743 through the standing stones, married the Highlander Jamie Fraser, survived the Jacobite rising, and was sent back pregnant on the eve of Culloden. Twenty years later she returned to a Jamie who had survived the battle, years as an outlaw and years in prison, and the two were shipwrecked into the American colonies, where they took a mountain land grant and founded Fraser's Ridge in North Carolina. Their daughter Brianna followed them through the stones to warn them of a newspaper notice reporting their deaths in a fire on the Ridge in 1776, and Roger Wakefield followed her. In Wilmington Brianna was raped by Stephen Bonnet, a pirate the Frasers had once helped escape hanging, and arrived pregnant, unable to say whether the child was Roger's or Bonnet's. Roger was mistaken for her attacker, beaten by Jamie and sold to the Mohawk; Jamie and Claire bought him back at the price of Young Ian, who stayed behind with the tribe. Roger came home, claimed Brianna's son Jemmy as his own, and the two were married. Bonnet is still alive.

In the autumn of 1770 the Frasers come down from the mountain to the annual Highland gathering at Mount Helicon, the one occasion in the year when a priest, a magistrate and every Scot in the colony can be found in the same place. Brianna and Roger, married by handfast, are wed properly, and Jemmy is baptised. Jamie's aunt Jocasta announces her betrothal to Duncan Innes. Claire works through a long queue of patients, among them a silent young hunter whose throat is rotting. The gathering also brings politics: the backcountry is in armed revolt, farmers calling themselves Regulators are seizing courts and beating sheriffs over corrupt fees and taxes, and Governor Tryon's man delivers Jamie's commission as a colonel of militia with orders to raise men against them. Jamie, who owes his land to the governor, cannot refuse.

Back on Fraser's Ridge the household expands: a new housekeeper and her husband take the place in hand, tenants arrive, and Claire's surgery and Brianna's workshop both grow. Roger, whose scholarship is worthless here, sets about learning to shoot, to work and to lead men, and begins to take services and sing for the settlement. When the governor's summons has to be answered, Jamie assembles the tenants, sets a wooden cross alight in the old Highland way, and takes their oaths to follow him as militia. Roger, who knows how the coming quarrel between the colonies and Britain ends, gives an oath to the Crown he does not believe in. Word also reaches the family that Stephen Bonnet is alive and doing business in the colony, which Brianna receives badly. She, meanwhile, produces matches, plans a water wheel, and adapts what she remembers of engineering to what the mountain can supply.

The militia rides out to gather men from the scattered backcountry settlements, and the campaign is more diplomacy than war: suspicious villages, drink, feuds, and Roger's first attempt at command, which goes badly. At Brownsville the company recruits reluctantly. Riding on, Jamie and Claire call at an isolated trading farm and find a household in which a man has been kept crippled and mute in a loft for months by his wife; he is beyond saving, and Jamie ends it. The wife gives birth and walks away, leaving the baby to be fostered out. Two indentured brothers from the same farm, Josiah and Keziah Beardsley, are freed and taken back toward the Ridge. Word comes that the Regulator emergency has passed for the season, and Jamie is able to send his men home without a battle.

Winter closes the mountain in. The Frasers keep Christmas and Hogmanay, the households on the Ridge settle into a routine of stock, food and sickness, and Claire's practice grows. Roger and Brianna's marriage steadies, and Jemmy thrives. Letters come up from the lowlands and from England, including from Jamie's old friend Lord John Grey, carrying news of what London is thinking about its colonies. Under all of it sit two things nobody says aloud: that Stephen Bonnet is somewhere in the colony, and that neither Roger nor Brianna knows whose son Jemmy is.

In the spring of 1771 the family travels down to River Run for Jocasta's wedding to Duncan Innes. The plantation is unsettled: a fortune in Jacobite gold that Jocasta's late husband carried out of Scotland is hidden somewhere, and other people know it, one of whom is found dead in the house. Duncan, on the eve of his marriage, confides a private difficulty about it to Claire and Jamie. The wedding goes ahead. Claire treats the household and the slaves, Brianna's dread of Bonnet resurfaces, and Roger continues to look for a use for himself. Then the political news turns: the Regulators have risen again in force, the governor has raised troops in earnest, and this time the militia will be marching to fight.

The militia marches with the governor's army to the Alamance river, where several thousand Regulators are camped. Jamie, who has no wish to fight farmers, sends Roger into the Regulator camp to look for a man and to carry word. On 16 May 1771 the two forces meet and the battle is short and one-sided: the Regulators are dispersed by artillery and disciplined fire within a couple of hours. In the aftermath the militia hangs several men taken for Regulators, and Roger, caught on the wrong side and unable to prove who he is, is among them. Jamie and Claire find him hours later, still just alive in the tree, and cut him down; Claire opens his windpipe with a knife to get air into him. He lives, but he cannot speak. Tryon has a prisoner executed as an example, and Jamie, having paid the governor everything he owed him and more, is finished with his service.

The family brings Roger home, and the long aftermath begins. He cannot talk, is in constant pain, and has lost the singing voice that was the one thing he could do better than anyone on the mountain; his rage and despair are hard on Brianna and on everyone else. Claire nurses him through the damage. Life on the Ridge resumes: harvest, patients, births, a new sword for Roger and lessons in using it, and letters from Lord John. A homestead not far off burns to the ground with a body inside, and the fire and the bones sit uncomfortably close to the printed notice that says Jamie and Claire will die that way. By slow degrees Roger begins to force out a whisper.

Roger's whisper becomes usable speech, ruined but serviceable, and he takes on the work of preaching, teaching and burying on the Ridge, deciding that a man can be of use without a voice worth hearing. He and Brianna face the question of the stones and choose to stay in the past, where their family is. The settlement grows: more tenants, more stock, Fergus and Marsali nearby, Claire's practice busier every season. Jemmy is a healthy toddler, and the matter of his father remains unsettled and largely unspoken. Beyond the mountain, the colony continues to drift toward open quarrel with Britain, and Stephen Bonnet is still alive.

The last movement of the book turns on gold and on Bonnet. Jocasta Cameron's hidden Jacobite fortune draws men to River Run, and Stephen Bonnet is one of them. Before the family can deal with it, Jamie is bitten by a venomous snake and comes as close to dying as he has ever come; Claire fights gangrene and fever for days and pulls him through. The pursuit of Bonnet ends on the coast at Wylie's Landing, in a running fight in which Brianna shoots him in the head at close range. He goes into the water and no body is recovered. The family returns to Fraser's Ridge: Roger with a whisper and a congregation, Brianna with a son whose parentage nobody will ever settle, Jamie alive and lame, and Claire holding a dated notice of their deaths that is still several years away. The book ends with Jamie telling Claire that if the day comes when he must leave her and his last words are not that he loves her, it will only be for want of breath to say them.

characters.description: A royal Moroi spirit user in his early twenties and one of this book's two narrators. He is in a secret relationship with an Alchemist, which is the first thing in his life he has genuinely wanted to be good for, and he is trying to build something worth showing her: painting seriously, taking a class, staying out of the bottle. He takes medication that steadies his moods but blocks his magic, so every use of spirit is a choice between being useful and being well - and spirit, over time, does not leave its users intact.
characters.name: Adrian Ivashkov

characters.description: The Alchemist running the Palm Springs assignment and this book's other narrator. She is a trained witch, secretly in love with a Moroi, secretly free of her tattoo's compulsion, and now living with her younger sister, who has been sent to watch her. Every day is an exercise in appearing to be exactly what her order expects while being none of it. She is also the only chemist the Moroi researchers have, and the work she is doing for them would be treason if the Alchemists understood it.
characters.name: Sydney Sage

characters.description: Sydney's younger sister, newly made an Alchemist and posted to Palm Springs as her partner and housemate. She is devout, eager and frightened of vampires exactly as she was trained to be, and she reports everything. She still wants her sister's approval, which is the one thing that makes her dangerous to lie to.
characters.name: Zoe Sage

characters.description: The Moroi queen's half-sister, still hidden at Amberwood, and now old enough to resent how much of her life is being managed for her. She is bonded to Adrian and feels everything he feels, which in a household full of secrets makes her the person least able to be told anything.
characters.name: Jill Dragomir

characters.description: Jill's dhampir guardian, still posing as her brother and still refusing to admit he wants anything for himself. He is with Angeline, and it is not going well.
characters.name: Eddie Castile

characters.description: The Keeper-raised dhampir attached to the household, impulsive, honest to a fault and badly matched to the life she has been dropped into. She is with Eddie and unhappy about it in ways she has not told him.
characters.name: Angeline Dawes

characters.description: Sydney's lab partner and former Warrior of Light, now cut off from his family and working an ordinary job. He keeps the group's secrets and has one of his own.
characters.name: Trey Juarez

characters.description: A young British dhampir guardian sent to reinforce the Palm Springs detail. Immaculately correct, humourless about duty and quietly formidable, he is admired by rather more of the household than he notices.
characters.name: Neil Raymond

characters.description: Sydney's teacher and the witch who trained her, now working with a student who has passed the point of needing to be persuaded. Her lessons have moved on to summonings and workings that require more than one caster.
characters.name: Jaclyn Terwilliger

characters.description: The former Alchemist who broke Sydney's tattoo, running his small group of defectors and pressing her again to leave the order rather than work inside it. He has plans elsewhere and does not intend to wait for her.
characters.name: Marcus Finch

characters.description: The Moroi spirit user and restored former Strigoi leading the research effort. She is trying to find something that would stop a Moroi or dhampir being turned at all, and Sydney's chemistry is what makes testing it possible.
characters.name: Sonya Karp

characters.description: A Moroi spirit user who joins the research, gentle and eager and openly interested in Adrian. She restored her own sister from Strigoi, which few spirit users have ever managed, and it left her with a bond and a great deal of guilt.
characters.name: Nina Sinclair

characters.description: The Alchemist Sydney exposed and had arrested. He has been through the order's re-education, and what came out the other side is a hollow, terrified man who cannot be alone in the dark and will not say plainly what was done to him.
characters.name: Keith Darnell

characters.description: A small scaled creature summoned in one of Ms. Terwilliger's workings, part lizard and part something else, which imprints on the two people who called it and has to be fed, carried and hidden. Harmless, demanding and inconveniently affectionate.
characters.name: Hopper

characters.description: Adrian's father: a wealthy, contemptuous royal Moroi who regards his son as an embarrassment and says so. His visits are brief and corrosive.
characters.name: Nathan Ivashkov

recaps.ending: The book ends on the disaster it has been building towards. Zoe finds out what her sister has been hiding - the relationship with Adrian, and everything it implies about Sydney's loyalty - and does what she was trained to do: she reports it. Sydney is taken by the Alchemists without warning, seized in daylight, her phone and her charms gone, and driven out into the desert to a place nobody outside the order knows the location of. She understands, from what she has already seen of Keith Darnell, precisely what re-education means and how little of a person it returns. Adrian is left behind knowing only that she is gone. He has no way to find her, no standing to demand anything from the Alchemists, and no protection from what losing her will do to a spirit user who has stopped taking his medication. The research into a defence against Strigoi conversion is unfinished, Jill is still in hiding, and the household's cover in Palm Springs is now compromised by the order that was supposed to be maintaining it.
recaps.in_short: Sydney and Adrian are together in secret while Sydney's newly minted Alchemist sister Zoe lives in the next room and reports on everything. The book alternates between them: Adrian trying to build a life worth offering her, painting, taking a class and weighing his medication against his access to spirit; Sydney hiding a relationship, a magical education and a research programme that would count as treason to her order. With Sonya Karp and the spirit user Nina Sinclair, they work towards something that would stop a Moroi or dhampir being turned Strigoi at all, and Sydney's chemistry is what makes it testable. They visit Keith Darnell and see what the Alchemists' re-education leaves of a person. They summon a small creature that bonds to them both. Adrian goes off his medication to use spirit properly and swings hard between elation and collapse; Angeline's secret with Trey ends her relationship with Eddie; Jill's isolation grows. Then Zoe learns the truth about her sister. In the final pages Sydney is seized by the Alchemists and taken away to be re-educated, and Adrian is left with no idea where she has gone.

recaps.text: Previously: Sydney Sage is an Alchemist - a member of a secret human order that hides vampires from the world - running the assignment that conceals Jill Dragomir, the Moroi queen's half-sister, at a human boarding school in Palm Springs. Jill lives as Sydney's sister and is guarded by the dhampirs Eddie Castile and Angeline Dawes; the royal Moroi Adrian Ivashkov, psychically bonded to Jill since he healed her, lives nearby. Over two years Sydney has exposed a corrupt Alchemist, stopped a restored Strigoi who was killing young Moroi women, helped rescue Sonya Karp from a society of human vampire hunters, and discovered that she is a witch, trained in secret by her teacher Jaclyn Terwilliger. She then learned from Marcus Finch, an Alchemist who escaped the order, that the golden lily tattoo every Alchemist wears carries compulsion that keeps them obedient; she had hers broken, and now passes as loyal while being nothing of the kind. She destroyed a witch who came for her power, and finally admitted what she felt for Adrian: they are together, secretly, in defiance of everything her order believes. At the same moment her younger sister Zoe, newly committed to the Alchemists, arrived in Palm Springs as her assigned partner.

Sydney and Adrian conduct a relationship in stolen hours and coded messages, because Zoe is now living with Sydney, watching everything, and reporting to their father and the order. Sydney has to hide three things at once: Adrian, her magic, and the fact that her tattoo no longer compels her. Adrian, who has never had a reason to be reliable before, is trying to be one - painting seriously, keeping his drinking down, and taking a class. A new guardian, Neil Raymond, arrives to reinforce the detail, impeccably correct and immediately the object of more attention than he realizes. Jill, bonded to Adrian, experiences a great deal that nobody is willing to explain to her, and Zoe's presence makes the whole household perform a version of itself.

The research restarts in earnest. Sonya Karp is pursuing something bigger than restoring Strigoi: a way to keep a Moroi or dhampir from being turned in the first place, and Sydney's chemistry is what makes it testable. Adrian's contribution requires spirit, and spirit requires him to stop taking the medication that keeps his moods level, so he goes off it - which restores his magic and takes away his floor. Marcus Finch resurfaces to press Sydney again to leave the order altogether, and leaves for his own work when she refuses; staying inside is still how she protects everyone. Ms. Terwilliger's lessons move on to workings that need two casters, and Sydney's competence has passed the point where she can call it an experiment.

Adrian's father visits and reduces everything his son has been building to a joke, which Adrian survives better than he expects and worse than he admits. Adrian's art class gives him the first genuine achievement of his life. Angeline's secret involvement with Trey comes out and ends her relationship with Eddie, leaving the household's fragile arrangement worse than before. Nina Sinclair joins the research: a spirit user who restored her own sister from Strigoi, one of the very few who have ever managed it, and who is plainly interested in Adrian.

Sydney and Adrian go to see Keith Darnell, the Alchemist Sydney exposed, to learn what the order actually does to the people it takes. What they find is a man who has been through re-education and come out hollow, frightened of the dark, unable to say plainly what happened to him. It is the clearest picture Sydney has of what waits for her if she is ever caught, and it does not change her mind about staying. He and Sydney also work one of Ms. Terwilliger's summonings together and end up jointly responsible for a small scaled creature that has bonded to both of them and has to be fed and hidden. The research edges towards a usable result. Off his medication, Adrian's magic works and his moods do not: he moves between long stretches of energy and productivity and drops he cannot explain away. He and Sydney tell each other what they feel without hedging it, which is the most dangerous thing either of them has done.

Zoe's suspicions harden. She has noticed the absences, the messages and her sister's unaccountable ease around Moroi, and she has been raised to treat all of it as evidence of corruption. Sydney manages her, deflects her and keeps her convinced, and each success buys less time than the last. Adrian's swings deepen, and Jill takes the worst of them through the bond while the household argues around her. The Strigoi research reaches the point of needing what only spirit can supply. Sydney is doing the work of an Alchemist, a witch, a chemist and a liar simultaneously, and the number of people who would have to be silenced to keep it hidden has grown past anything she can control.

Zoe learns the truth about her sister and Adrian, and reports it. Sydney is seized by the Alchemists in daylight, stripped of her phone and her charms before she can use anything, and driven away into the desert to a facility whose location nobody outside the order knows. She knows exactly what is waiting, because she has seen what re-education left of Keith Darnell. Adrian is left behind with no way to find her, no standing to make demands of the Alchemists, and no medication in his system to absorb the loss. Jill is still hiding, the research is unfinished, and the Palm Springs arrangement has been broken open by the order that was supposed to be maintaining it.

characters.description: A woman who rejects the fashionable informality and smaller families of her generation in favor of a large household organized around marriage, children, and family gatherings. Harriet's certainty is tested by a terrifying fifth pregnancy and by her conviction that the child others reject still remains her responsibility.
characters.name: Harriet Lovatt

characters.description: Harriet's husband, who shares her dream of a stable, crowded family home. David is initially confident that love and conventional domestic life will protect them, but fear of his fifth son drives a widening division between him and Harriet.
characters.name: David Lovatt

characters.description: Harriet and David's fifth child. Ben is abnormally strong and difficult even before birth, then develops into a watchful, powerful boy whose needs and behavior resist the family's expectations. The adults around him struggle to decide whether he is ill, dangerous, misunderstood, or fundamentally unlike them.
characters.name: Ben Lovatt

characters.description: Harriet and David's eldest child, born into the warm and busy household they deliberately create. As Ben comes to dominate family life, Luke is among the older children whose security and willingness to remain at home are damaged.
characters.name: Luke Lovatt

characters.description: One of Harriet and David's older children. Helen grows up amid the large holiday gatherings that define the family's early happiness, then shares her siblings' fear and resentment as the atmosphere of the house changes.
characters.name: Helen Lovatt

characters.description: Harriet and David's third child, part of the close group of siblings born before Ben. Jane's childhood is shaped first by the family's confidence and later by the precautions and divided loyalties created by her youngest brother.
characters.name: Jane Lovatt

characters.description: The youngest of the four children born before Ben. Paul receives less attention as Harriet struggles through her next pregnancy and its aftermath, and his unhappiness becomes another cost of the family's concentration on Ben.
characters.name: Paul Lovatt

characters.description: Harriet's mother, who provides practical help as births and large family visits strain the Lovatt household. Dorothy sees both Harriet's exhaustion and the danger surrounding Ben, and her support does not prevent painful disagreement about what should be done.
characters.name: Dorothy

characters.description: David's wealthy father, whose money helps sustain the large house and the family-centered life Harriet and David could not otherwise afford. His assistance also reveals how much their supposed independence rests on relatives they expect to gather around them.
characters.name: James Lovatt

characters.description: A young man on the margins of conventional life who can communicate with Ben more easily than Ben's family can. John and his companions accept Ben into their rough group without demanding that he behave like an ordinary Lovatt child.
characters.name: John

recaps.ending: After Harriet brings Ben back from the institution, the Lovatt family does not recover its earlier unity. The older children arrange to spend more time away, Paul remains troubled, and David regards Harriet's choice as the act that destroyed their remaining chance of ordinary family life. Ben grows into a powerful adolescent who is increasingly detached from the household. He finds a place among John and other rootless young people, follows them rather than Harriet, and eventually goes away with them. Harriet is left with neither the crowded family center she wanted nor certainty about Ben's future. Watching reports of violent crowds on television, she searches the faces and wonders whether Ben has joined such a group. The book closes without confirming where he is, leaving Harriet to confront both his unknowability and the collapse of the domestic ideal on which she and David built their lives.
recaps.in_short: Harriet and David Lovatt marry with a shared dream of a large, traditional family and buy a spacious house that becomes the center of happy gatherings. Four children are born in quick succession. Harriet's fifth pregnancy is violently different, and Ben arrives early, unusually strong, watchful, and difficult to control. Fear of him drives relatives away and makes the older children feel unsafe. Under pressure, the family sends Ben to an institution, but Harriet is horrified by its brutal neglect and brings him home. That rescue permanently divides her from David and the other children. Ben later attaches himself to a group of troubled youths led by John and eventually leaves with them. The Lovatt household disperses, the marriage is damaged, and Harriet remains unsure whether she saved Ben or sacrificed everyone else to a duty only she would accept.

recaps.text: Harriet and David Lovatt meet, marry, and deliberately build the kind of domestic life they believe modern society has undervalued. With financial help from David's father they buy a large house, have four children in quick succession, and host extended family for long, crowded holidays. Their apparent success depends heavily on relatives' money, labor, and continued willingness to gather. A fifth pregnancy violently disrupts this order. Harriet experiences the unborn child as abnormally strong and hostile, and Ben is born early, powerful, hungry, and difficult to soothe. As he grows, his physical force, emotional distance, and attacks on animals and other children make the household afraid. Relatives stop visiting, the older children avoid him, and David increasingly sees Ben as an intruder who has destroyed the family. The adults eventually send the boy to an institution. When Harriet visits, she finds him drugged, restrained, and wasting away among severely neglected children. She brings him home against the wishes of David and the wider family. Her decision saves Ben from that immediate fate but completes the fracture of the household: the older children leave when they can, Paul remains emotionally damaged, and David cannot forgive her. Ben grows into an alienated adolescent and finds companionship with John and a group of rough young people who accept his strength and strangeness. He eventually leaves with them. Harriet ends alone with her uncertainty, watching televised disorder and wondering whether one of the barely seen figures might be her son.

characters.description: Commander of the Ankh-Morpork City Watch and Duke of Ankh, a blunt, working-class copper who dislikes his own title and distrusts diplomacy. Lord Vetinari sends him abroad as an ambassador to the distant, dangerous country of Uberwald, a role he is spectacularly unsuited for and which he treats, at heart, as police work.
characters.name: Sam Vimes

characters.description: Vimes's wife, a large, warm, immensely capable aristocrat and famous breeder of swamp dragons. Well-connected and unflappable, she accompanies Vimes on his diplomatic mission and handles the social side of it far more gracefully than he does.
characters.name: Sybil Vimes

characters.description: A very tall man raised by dwarfs and a captain of the City Watch, honest and literal-minded, with a natural gift for leadership. He is romantically attached to the werewolf Angua.
characters.name: Carrot Ironfoundersson

characters.description: A sergeant of the City Watch and a werewolf, originally from an aristocratic werewolf family in Uberwald that she left behind. Capable and self-controlled, she is uneasy about the prospect of her homeland and her relatives re-entering her life.
characters.name: Angua von Uberwald

characters.description: A dwarf member of the Watch who works on forensic detection and who, unusually for a dwarf, openly presents as female. Precise and clever, she travels with Vimes into dwarf country, where such openness is provocative.
characters.name: Cheery Littlebottom

characters.description: A stout, cautious sergeant of the Watch who is left in charge of policing Ankh-Morpork while his superiors are abroad, a responsibility that quickly reveals the limits of his leadership.
characters.name: Fred Colon

characters.description: A scruffy, opportunistic corporal of the Watch of dubious pedigree, who carries a document certifying that he is human. He remains behind in the city with the skeleton Watch.
characters.name: Nobby Nobbs

characters.description: A troll sergeant of the City Watch, hugely strong and slower-witted in the heat, who accompanies Vimes on the journey to Uberwald as bodyguard and muscle.
characters.name: Detritus

characters.description: A scruffy, disreputable Ankh-Morpork street dog who can talk, a fact he keeps quiet. Cynical and streetwise, he attaches himself to the story as it moves and offers unsolicited canine commentary.
characters.name: Gaspode

characters.description: The dwarf about to be crowned ruler of the dwarfs at a grand coronation in Uberwald, a moment of high political tension. The ceremony depends on an ancient dwarf artefact of deep symbolic importance.
characters.name: The Low King

characters.description: Angua's brother, a powerful and aggressive werewolf of the Uberwald aristocracy who leads his family's clan. Physically imposing and openly contemptuous of weakness, he treats hunting and dominance as sport.
characters.name: Wolfgang von Uberwald

characters.description: A servant of the traditional Uberwald type, an Igor: lisping, scarred, endlessly helpful, and a master of surgery and stitchwork. He is assigned to assist Vimes at the embassy.
characters.name: Igor

recaps.ending: Vimes exposes the plot behind the theft of the Scone of Stone: a faction of traditionalist dwarfs arranged the crime and a forged replacement to control the succession. The forger's work is revealed, and the Low King, Rhys Rhysson, is properly crowned, using the moment to make a startling public admission about the relic that defuses its power as a weapon. Wolfgang von Uberwald, having hunted Vimes across the frozen countryside, is defeated, ending the werewolf clan's bid for dominance. Angua and Carrot reconcile and return together to Ankh-Morpork and the Watch. Vimes, glad to be done with diplomacy, heads home, where the chaos Colon caused is quietly undone. Lady Sybil shares happy news with Vimes: she is expecting their first child. Ankh-Morpork's interests in Uberwald are secured, and Vimes returns to the job he actually wants.
recaps.in_short: Lord Vetinari sends Commander Vimes to the wild country of Uberwald as Ankh-Morpork's ambassador, ostensibly for the coronation of a new dwarf Low King but really to secure trade in the region's fat and mineral wealth. Vimes, his wife Lady Sybil, and a small party of watchmen arrive to find the dwarfs in crisis: the Scone of Stone, the ancient relic on which the Low King is crowned, has been stolen. Vimes treats the diplomatic emergency as a criminal investigation, tangling with scheming deep-down dwarfs, vampires, and the werewolf clan of Uberwald, led by Angua's violent brother Wolfgang. Angua returns home ahead of the others and Carrot resigns from the Watch to follow her. Back in Ankh-Morpork, the Watch nearly falls apart under Colon's mismanagement. Vimes uncovers that the theft is part of a plot to control who becomes Low King, survives a lethal hunt across the snow, and exposes the conspiracy in time for the true relic's fate to be revealed and the rightful coronation to proceed.

recaps.text: Previously, in earlier books: Sam Vimes rose from a broken-down captain to Commander of the Ankh-Morpork City Watch and, by marrying the aristocratic dragon-breeder Lady Sybil, became Duke of Ankh. He built the Watch into a large, mixed force of humans, dwarfs, trolls, and others, among them Captain Carrot, a human raised by dwarfs who is rumoured to have a claim to the city's vacant throne but prefers to stay a watchman, and Sergeant Angua, a werewolf who left her homeland behind. In a recent crisis, when a risen island nearly triggered a war between Ankh-Morpork and the empire of Klatch, Vimes refused to treat murder as patriotism and helped stop the conflict before it began. As this book opens, he is a reluctant fixture of the city's ruling class, still happiest working as a policeman.

Lord Vetinari appoints Commander Vimes, to his dismay, as Ankh-Morpork's ambassador to Uberwald, a remote and dangerous land of dwarfs, vampires, and werewolves. The official occasion is the coronation of a new dwarf Low King; the real business is trade and influence over the region's valuable resources. Vimes and Lady Sybil prepare to travel far from the city Vimes knows, into a place where he has no authority and few of the rules he relies on apply.

characters.description: A woman in her forties living quietly in the small southern comm of Tirimo, where she teaches at the creche. She is an orogene: she can sense and shape the movement of the earth, a power the Stillness fears and usually answers with a lynching, so she has hidden it for years from her neighbors and from her husband. She taught both her children in secret, and harshly, to hide what they inherited from her. The book opens on the day she comes home to find her three-year-old son beaten to death and her husband and daughter gone, and on the day a rift opens across the width of the continent and begins a Season that may not end in her lifetime.
characters.name: Essun

characters.description: Essun's three-year-old son, a talkative and unusually quick child who had already begun to show orogeny at home. His father kills him before the book opens, and Essun sits with his body for two days before she can make herself move.
characters.name: Uche

characters.description: Essun's husband, a stone-knapper in Tirimo who works flint and glass and is well liked in the comm. Until the day the book opens he was an affectionate father. On discovering that his younger child was an orogene, he beat the boy to death and left the comm with their daughter.
characters.name: Jija

characters.description: Essun's daughter, a watchful, self-possessed girl who inherited her mother's orogeny and was drilled in secret to keep it hidden and controlled. She is not in Tirimo when the book opens: her father has taken her south. Finding her alive is the reason Essun leaves home at all.
characters.name: Nassun

characters.description: A girl from a small northern village who is locked in her family's barn after her orogeny surfaces in front of the other children at school. Her parents have sent for someone to take her away. Proud, stubborn, and quick to reason her way through a bad situation, she understands that her family has given her up and is trying to work out what she is worth to anyone now. She is bright, she does not cry where people can see her, and she wants very badly to be kept.
characters.name: Damaya

characters.description: A Guardian, one of the order that finds orogene children and delivers them to the Fulcrum or kills them where they stand. He arrives to collect Damaya: an enormous man with long black hair, pale eyes, and an easy affectionate manner that never quite matches what he does. He is genuinely warm toward the frightened child in his care and also, calmly, brutal with her, and explains both as necessary. Guardians can shut off an orogene's power with a touch, which is why the Fulcrum's orogenes obey.
characters.name: Schaffa

characters.description: Tirimo's doctor, a serious young man who grew up in the comm, trained elsewhere, and came back to it. He is one of the few people who treats Essun as a person rather than a rumor once the town turns suspicious, and he makes it clear that what she is does not surprise him.
characters.name: Lerna

characters.description: A four-ring orogene of the Fulcrum, the imperial institution in the capital that trains, houses and rents out the orogenes it can catch. She is competent, sharp-tongued, and impatient for the rings that would bring her better work and more freedom. The assignment she is given instead is a humiliation: clear a silted harbor in a provincial coastal city, in the company of the Fulcrum's most senior orogene, and conceive a child by him on the way, because the Fulcrum breeds its orogenes as deliberately as it trains them.
characters.name: Syenite

characters.description: The Fulcrum's only ten-ring orogene, far more powerful than anyone Syenite has met and used by the institution as both a tool and a stud. He is theatrical, sardonic, and openly contemptuous of the rules and deference that structure Syenite's whole life, which makes him exhausting to travel with. He appears unstable and half broken, and he is nevertheless right about a great many things she was never allowed to learn.
characters.name: Alabaster

characters.description: A small boy Essun finds on the road south: naked, filthy, entirely unafraid, with white hair, white skin and eyes like clear ice. He gives his name as Hoa, will not say where he came from, and attaches himself to her journey on the claim that he can help her find her daughter. He does not eat ordinary food, is stronger and stranger than a child should be, and knows things about the roads, and about Essun, that he has no way of knowing.
characters.name: Hoa

characters.description: A filthy, foul-tempered commless traveler who takes up with Essun and Hoa on the road south and will not be shaken off. She is educated far past anything a road scavenger should be, obsessively interested in obelisks and in ancient ruins, evasive about where her learning came from, and unnervingly curious about Essun in particular.
characters.name: Tonkee

characters.description: A stone eater: one of the rare statue-like beings who move through solid rock as easily as a person walks through air, hold impossible stillness between one moment and the next, and take an interest in orogenes for reasons they decline to explain. She gives her name as Antimony, fixes her attention on Alabaster, and does not leave.
characters.name: Antimony

characters.description: A girl of a wealthy Leadership family in the capital who bribes and lies her way onto the Fulcrum's grounds while Damaya is training there. She is not an orogene. She is looking for something the city's oldest records say lies beneath the compound and that no one in authority will admit exists.
characters.name: Binof

characters.description: The leader of Meov, an island comm whose people live by raiding the ships that pass their stretch of coast. He is huge, loud and generous, and he is an orogene who was never taken by a Guardian and never trained by the Fulcrum, self-taught in ways the Fulcrum insists are impossible and unashamed of any of it.
characters.name: Innon

characters.description: The son born to Syenite and Alabaster on Meov: a calm, strong child raised beyond the Fulcrum's reach, and powerful from the moment he can reach for anything at all.
characters.name: Corundum

characters.description: The headwoman of Castrima, a comm built underground inside a geode. She is openly an orogene, recruits others instead of hiding them, and holds together a settlement in which orogenes and ordinary people share the same space, which nowhere else on the continent manages. Self-taught, dry, and relentlessly practical about what the arrangement costs.
characters.name: Ykka

recaps.ending:
Meov, the island comm where Syenite has lived free for two years, is found. A Guardian ship arrives, Schaffa among the boarding party, and Guardians can switch an orogene off by touch. Innon is killed in the fighting. Antimony takes Alabaster away through the rock. Cornered, and certain that Schaffa intends to carry her infant son off to a node station and wire him into a chair, Syenite kills Corundum herself, then reaches through a garnet obelisk and destroys Meov and everyone left on it. She survives, walks away from the wreck of her life, and starts again under another new name.

The three threads are one life. Damaya became Syenite; Syenite became Essun. The woman in Tirimo is the girl from the barn and the Fulcrum orogene, decades apart, renamed each time she had to begin again. The man who tore the continent open in the prologue is Alabaster.

In the present, Essun, Hoa and Tonkee reach Castrima, a comm hidden inside a geode underground and led openly by an orogene named Ykka. Alabaster is there: most of his body already turned to stone, the rest being consumed by Antimony. He admits that he opened the Rift deliberately, that the Seasons are an injury rather than a fact of nature, and that he needs Essun to finish what he began. His question closes the book: has she ever heard of a thing called a moon. Jija and Nassun are still alive somewhere to the south, and Essun has not stopped looking.
recaps.in_short: The Stillness is a continent whose civilizations are periodically ended by seismic catastrophe, and whose orogenes, people who can still or start earthquakes, are feared, owned and killed. Three stories run in parallel: Damaya, a girl handed to a Guardian and raised in the imperial Fulcrum; Syenite, a Fulcrum orogene sent on assignment with the powerful, insubordinate Alabaster and shown by him how much the empire hides; and Essun, a middle-aged woman in a small comm who comes home to find her small son murdered by her husband and her daughter taken, on the same day an orogene tears a rift across the continent and begins a Season expected to last centuries. Syenite's thread ends with a free comm destroyed by Guardians, her lover dead, and Syenite killing her own infant son rather than let him be enslaved. The three women are one: Damaya became Syenite, Syenite became Essun. Essun reaches the underground comm of Castrima and finds Alabaster there, dying and half turned to stone. He admits he broke the world on purpose, and asks whether she has ever heard of a thing called a moon.

recaps.text:
The Stillness is a single continent shaken so regularly that every institution on it is organized around survival: comms stockpile against Fifth Seasons, the long ash winters that end eras, and stonelore tells everyone how to live through one. Orogenes can sense and control the movement of the earth. They are hated and commonly killed on discovery; the empire of Sanze controls the ones it catches through the Fulcrum, an institution in the capital of Yumenes, and through the Guardians, who collect orogene children and can shut their power off with a touch.

The book opens with two endings. In Yumenes, a man of extraordinary power tears a rift across the width of the continent, destroying the capital and beginning a Season that will last centuries. In the small southern comm of Tirimo, a woman named Essun comes home to find her three-year-old son Uche beaten to death by her husband Jija, who has taken their daughter Nassun and gone. Essun is an orogene who has hidden it for years, and so were her children. When the shockwave from the north reaches Tirimo she instinctively turns it aside from the comm, and the town, which now suspects what she is, becomes dangerous to her. She buries her son and leaves through the gate, heading south after Jija and Nassun.

Elsewhere in the Stillness, a girl named Damaya is locked in her parents' barn after her orogeny surfaces at school. A Guardian named Schaffa comes for her and takes her away.

Essun travels south on the Imperial Road as ash begins to fall from the north and comms shut their gates against strangers. She is joined by a small boy who calls himself Hoa: white-haired, white-eyed, afraid of nothing on the road, who says he can help her find her daughter and will not say where he came from.

Schaffa takes Damaya north toward Yumenes. On the way he deliberately breaks her hand, then sets it and tends her, explaining that she has to learn she cannot hurt him and that he will hurt her whenever it is necessary. He also tells her what she is worth: an orogene is a tool that can save a comm or destroy one, and the Fulcrum exists to make the difference reliable. Damaya, discarded by her family, decides to become worth keeping.

In Yumenes, Syenite is a four-ring orogene of the Fulcrum, proud of her rank and impatient for more. She is handed an assignment she resents: travel to the coastal city of Allia and clear its silted harbor, in the company of Alabaster, the Fulcrum's only ten-ringer, and conceive a child by him on the way, because the Fulcrum breeds its orogenes as deliberately as it trains them. Alabaster proves to be powerful beyond anything she has seen, openly contemptuous of the rules she has built her life on, and apparently unstable.

Damaya arrives at the Fulcrum and is enrolled as a grit, the lowest rank, in a compound where orogene children are drilled in control, punished hard for failure, and reminded constantly that every one of them was given up by their family. Rings are earned by examination and mark rank. The Guardians are always present.

Syenite and Alabaster travel toward Allia. He is exhausting company, and he shows her things the Fulcrum never taught: that orogeny can be done with a precision she was told was impossible, and that the empire's remarkable seismic stability is paid for. At a node station along the road they find the maintainer, an orogene child mutilated and wired into a chair, kept alive to quell shakes automatically for the region around it. The station's attendant is missing and the maintainer is dead. Syenite understands that this is where the Fulcrum's failures go, and that any child of hers could end there.

Essun goes on south with Hoa through thickening ashfall, past comms that have already closed and settlements already emptied. She avoids the trouble she can and keeps moving toward the roads her husband is most likely to have taken.

Syenite and Alabaster reach Allia, a coastal city that resents needing them, and clear the blocked harbor. In the seabed Syenite finds something that should not be there: a broken obelisk, one of the enormous crystals that drift unexplained above the continent, sunken and buried, with the body of a stone eater inside it. Alabaster reacts with real fear and will not fully explain why. Their standing with Allia's leadership deteriorates from there.

At the Fulcrum, Damaya learns the institution's real curriculum: absolute control, absolute obedience to Guardians, and the understanding that an orogene's life is held on sufferance. She trains, makes a few careful friendships among the other grits, and works toward her first ring.
